A Tax With Cliffs

HAWAIʻI TAXES EVERY SALE OF REAL PROPERTY when the deed is recorded. The rate depends on the price and applies to the whole of it, so the tax jumps at each threshold: a home that sells for $3,999,000 pays 0.5 percent, or $19,995, and one that sells for $4,000,000 pays 0.7 percent, or $28,000. Buyers who cannot claim a county homeowner exemption, because the home will not be their main residence, pay a slightly higher schedule (Table 1).1

The tax raised $96 million in fiscal year 2025.2 The first 10 percent, up to $5.1 million, goes to the land conservation fund and half, up to $38 million, to the rental housing revolving fund. The rest goes to the general fund.3

Today’s rate applies to the whole price of a sale in the band. The draft’s rate applies only to the part of the price within the band, and the total is capped at 4 percent of the price for owner-occupants and 6 percent for other buyers. Today’s owner-occupant schedule also covers commercial, agricultural and other nonresidential property, and the draft keeps it for them.

What SB 3028 Would Change

THE LAST DRAFT OF SB 3028 would tax home sales the way the income tax taxes income: each rate applies only to the part of the price within its band.4 For a buyer who will live in the home, the part of the price between $2 million and $3 million would be taxed at 2 percent and the part between $3 million and $6 million at 4 percent. For other buyers, those rates would be 5 percent and 7 percent. The band edges would rise each year with consumer prices, starting in 2027. Nonresidential property would stay on today’s schedule.

Because the rates below $2 million would change little and apply only to each slice of the price, the draft cuts the tax on every owner-occupied sale under $2,247,000 and every other home sale under $2,073,000. Above those prices it raises the tax, steeply (Table 2). House Finance Committee Chair Chris Todd gave the same thresholds, about $2.3 million and $2.1 million, when his committee approved the draft on April 2, 2026.5

House and Senate negotiators met through May 1 without agreeing, and the bill died with the session.6 The draft is the fullest statement of where the Legislature left the idea, and the model scores its rates as written, as if enacted in 2027.

Who Would Pay More

MOST SALES WOULD PAY THE SAME OR LESS. Maui is the one county that publishes every sale with its price and the conveyance tax paid.7 Of its sales in recent years, 43 percent would pay less under the draft and 42 percent the same, mostly because they are nonresidential or sell for less than $600,000. The other 15 percent would pay more.

Nearly all of the new revenue would come from the top of the market. On Maui, sales above $4 million would provide 88 percent of it, and buyers who will not make the home their main residence 90 percent. Chair Todd put the statewide share of sales paying the same or less at 91 percent. Maui’s share is lower because it has more expensive sales than the rest of the state, relative to its size.

The $3 Million to $4 Million Home

A HOME SELLING FOR $3.5 MILLION to a family that will live in it pays $17,500 in conveyance tax today. Under the draft it would pay $46,300. Sold to anyone else, it would pay $93,800 instead of $21,000. This is where the draft turns steep: at $3 million the rate on each added dollar jumps to 4 percent for owner-occupants and 7 percent for other buyers, while today’s rate holds at 0.5 or 0.6 percent of the price up to $4 million.

At fiscal year 2028 prices, about 72 Maui homes a year sell for $3 million to $4 million, 52 of them to buyers who will not live in them. Those buyers’ average tax would rise from $20,554 to $84,132. For owner-occupants it would rise from $16,915 to $38,981. Even so, the band provides only 10 percent of Maui’s new revenue, because far more money changes hands above it (Figure 1).

The draft also ends today’s cliff at $4 million. Under it, a sale at $3,999,000 and one at $4,000,000 would owe almost the same, $66,260 and $66,300 for an owner-occupant, where today they differ by $8,005. These are the amounts due at the sale; part of a tax on sales can be passed back to sellers through the price.

What It Would Raise

STATEWIDE, THE DRAFT WOULD RAISE an estimated $69 million to $118 million more than current law in fiscal year 2028, the first full year a bill passed in 2027 could reach. That is on top of about $116 million the tax would raise anyway. Before accounting for fewer sales, the increase would be $113 million to $195 million.8

Transfer taxes discourage sales. Toronto’s 1.1 percent land transfer tax cut sales of single-family homes by about 15 percent,9 and a 1-point cut in the United Kingdom’s transaction tax raised short-run sales activity by about 20 percent.10 The estimates assume sales fall 10 percent for each point of the price the draft adds in tax, and rise where it cuts the tax. A response of 5 to 15 percent instead widens the range to $52 million to $153 million.

The range comes from how the rest of the state compares with Maui. The upper estimate assumes other counties’ sales are shaped like Maui’s, relative to the tax each already pays. The lower estimate uses 2025 counts of sales above $3 million on Oʻahu and Kauaʻi, which suggest the rest of the state has less than half as many, relative to its tax, as Maui does.11

Revenue grows faster than home prices, because as prices rise, more of each sale falls in the higher bands. Indexing the bands to consumer prices slows this but does not stop it while home prices rise faster, as the model assumes (4 percent a year against 3 percent). By fiscal year 2031 the increase reaches $77 million to $133 million (Figure 3).

Scored without a change in sales, at 2023 to 2025 prices, this model’s upper estimate is $151 million.

Where the Money Would Go

THE DRAFT ALSO REWRITES who gets the money. Before any reaches the general fund, it would send 5 percent, up to $10 million, to the land conservation fund; 20 percent, up to $40 million, to the rental housing revolving fund; 30 percent, up to $60 million, to the Hawaiian home lands infrastructure and housing special fund; and 20 percent, up to $40 million, to transit-oriented development infrastructure.4

Those shares add up to 75 percent of all conveyance tax, including the tax on sales the draft leaves unchanged, until the funds reach their caps. The general fund therefore comes out ahead only if the draft raises more than about $107 million a year. At the upper estimate it would receive $84 million in fiscal year 2028, $12 million more than under current law. At the lower estimate it would receive $46 million, $27 million less (Table 5).

How These Estimates Are Made

BECAUSE TODAY’S TWO SCHEDULES DIFFER, the tax recorded on a Maui sale shows which one applied, and so whether the buyer could claim a homeowner exemption. Of sales with a price and tax in fiscal years 2023 to 2026, 97 percent match one schedule to within half a percent; the rest are treated as nonresidential, whose tax the draft leaves alone. The county’s land-use codes separate owner-occupied homes from nonresidential property on the owner-occupant schedule. Applied to the sorted home sales, current law reproduces the tax Maui recorded on them to within a few hundred dollars a year. The model uses about 2,680 sales a year in all.7

No other county publishes its sales this way, so statewide figures scale Maui’s up by the Department of Taxation’s conveyance collections. Maui recorded 18 to 26 percent of the state’s conveyance tax in fiscal years 2023 to 2025.2 Each year’s sales are aged to future prices at 4 percent a year and scored separately, and the results are averaged, so that a few sales above $10 million in any one year do not drive the estimate.

Left out: the draft’s rule that apartment buildings be taxed unit by unit, which would lower their tax and so the estimate somewhat; long-term leases; a rush of sales before the law takes effect; and any effect on prices. The full method and every parameter are in the source code.8
